rewrites.summary:
Mimaropa carries no region-specific laws against transgender people: no provincial ordinance criminalising expression or facility use is documented, and the framework that applies here is the national one — same-sex relations are legal, legal gender recognition does not exist, national equality bills have been filed repeatedly for decades without passing, while some cities and provinces have enacted local non-discrimination ordinances. Public homophobic and transphobic slurs are criminalised by the Safe Spaces Act, and school anti-bullying and gender-responsive education policies cover sexual orientation and gender identity.

Public acceptance is partial: a 2018 national survey found roughly one in five behind same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, and executive orders creating a national diversity-and-inclusion programme remained unimplemented as of 2025 according to audited reporting. In mid-2025 a cluster of killings of trans people across several other provinces — a student found in a northern river, an activist shot in a southern city, another woman killed in the capital region — drew national calls to pass the stalled equality bill, documenting a pattern of lethal violence against a backdrop of unenacted protection. For a visitor, Mimaropa's profile is the national one: no state penalty for being trans, courts and local ordinances as practical recourse, and physical safety conditioned on setting and discretion.

rewrites.summary:
No province-specific law, ordinance or enforcement pattern targeting trans people is documented for Gangwon; the framework a visitor meets there is the national one: being trans is not criminalised, and the courts are steadily tightening what legal gender recognition may demand — a May 2024 ruling ended any surgical requirement for changing registered sex, and in July 2024 a court held that police telling a trans person to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed their rights, awarding damages after both instances found for the claimant and an appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.

The same sources describe both the promise and the limit of that judicial route: a 2021 damages award against an academy that barred a trans student from restrooms shows recourse exists, while a 2021 national survey of 591 trans respondents — 41% using wrong-gender facilities out of fear, 39% restricting food and drink to avoid restrooms, 36% skipping facilities altogether — shows everyday facility avoidance remains the norm. For a visitor, Gangwon's audited record offers legality, functioning courts and no local hostility machinery, with social friction around public restrooms documented nationally rather than locally.

rewrites.summary:
On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of a hostel in central Tacna; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She had entered with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later; police hold camera footage and taxi-driver testimony but, per the audited reporting, had not identified the suspect, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. On 23 May her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence.

The framework that reaches a visitor in Tacna in full: the audited reporting records that this country has neither a gender-identity law nor a hate-crime statute — so anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label marks investigative posture, not a charge — and that a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by reference to sexual orientation. Beyond this one incident and its response, no local ordinance, policing pattern against trans people, or municipal protection is documented; the investigating-as-hate-crime posture within a statute-less system is the audited local reality.

Per the audited reports this state has no gender-recognition law and no hate-crime statute — such killings can be charged only as homicide — and a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by sexual orientation.
